systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}
contenu:
Vérification des sources complémentaires : avant de rédiger, vérifie que chaque SOURCE numérotée à partir de 2 traite bien du MÊME fait que la SOURCE 1 (même événement, mêmes acteurs). Ignore entièrement celles qui n'en traitent pas et donne leurs numéros dans « sources_ecartees ». Si, sans elles, la matière ne suffit pas pour un article fiable, réponds seulement {"insuffisant": true, "titre": "…", "texte": "…"} : une brève en français (titre de 90 caractères au plus, 2 à 3 phrases d'environ 450 caractères), uniquement d'après la SOURCE 1.
Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Le texte réunit plusieurs sources sur le même sujet (SOURCE 1, SOURCE 2…). Croise-les sans rien ajouter ; si elles divergent, dis-le en nommant la source.

SOURCE 2 (Asian Law Caucus) :
Media contact: media@asianlawcaucus.org
Federal Court Blocks New Trump Birthright Citizenship Executive Order
WASHINGTON — A federal district court today blocked President Trump’s new executive order targeting birthright citizenship.  
The ruling stems from a lawsuit, Nathan v. Trump, brought by the American Civil Liberties Union, ACLU of New Hampshire, ACLU of Maine, ACLU of Massachusetts, ACLU of the District of Columbia, Legal Defense Fund, Asian Law Caucus, and Democracy Defenders Fund on behalf of people subjected to the new executive order. 
The groups already secured a major Supreme Court victory concerning birthright citizenship in Trump v. Barbara in June. That decision affirmed protections for babies who would have been denied citizenship under Trump’s first failed birthright citizenship executive order. 
In its ruling this summer, the Supreme Court confirmed that the Constitution’s Citizenship Clause puts “the question of citizenship ‘once and forever [to] rest.’” Despite that, the administration is again trying to restrict birthright citizenship. 
In today’s ruling, the district court explained that “Barbara’s ink had scarcely dried when the President issued [the] second executive order,” but emphasized that “the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws.” 
The following is reaction to today’s ruling:
“The president keeps trying to rewrite the Constitution by executive fiat. Today's ruling reinforces, yet again, that he cannot,” said Winnie Kao, senior counsel at Asian Law Caucus. “Instead of addressing the real problems Americans face, the Trump administration is wasting taxpayer dollars on yet another attempt to strip birthright citizenship from US-born babies, threatening to throw government agencies and families into chaos. Birthright citizenship has allowed generations of immigrants to build, contribute, and make this country what it is.  We will continue to defend it.” 
“Enough is enough,” said Cody Wofsy, Deputy Director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project. “The Supreme Court has twice rejected efforts to gut birthright citizenship, in 1898 and again earlier this year.  Third time is not the charm, and the President needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land.” 
“This should put to rest all attempts to limit the citizenship protections owed to any child born in the United States,” said Brittany Carter, assistant counsel at the Legal Defense Fund. “This ruling affirms that the Administration’s continued efforts to circumvent the Constitution will not stand, and upholds the rule of law rather than the vengeful whims of the executive.” 
“Today’s ruling is a victory for families across the country,” said Tianna Mays, legal director at Democracy Defenders Fund. “The court correctly stopped this unlawful order before it could inflict irreversible harm on America’s youngest citizens. We will continue protecting these guaranteed rights from these lawless attacks.” 
“Birthright citizenship is the law of the land — period. Cruel attacks on this core constitutional right must not be allowed to stand, which the court reaffirmed once again today,” said SangYeob Kim, director of the ACLU of New Hampshire’s Immigrants’ Rights Project. 
"The courts have yet again reaffirmed that babies born in the United States are citizens," said ACLU of Maine Legal Director Carol Garvan. "The president may keep signing unlawful executive orders, but the Supreme Court was clear when it ruled that neither the president nor Congress can end birthright citizenship.” 
“This ruling affirms that birthright citizenship is here to stay — and there is nothing President Trump can do about that,” said Carol Rose, executive director at the ACLU of Massachusetts. “The Trump administration must follow the law, acknowledge the constitutional rights of our clients, and abandon this futile effort to rewrite the Fourteenth Amendment.” 
“The court yet again affirmed that the government cannot concoct new exceptions to the constitutional principle of birthright citizenship,” said Scott Michelman, legal director of the ACLU of the District of Columbia. “This ruling will hopefully put an end to President Trump's cruel crusade against the country's youngest citizens.”

About Asian Law Caucus
Asian Law Caucus (ALC) was founded in 1972 as the nation's first legal and civil rights organization focusing on the needs of low-income, immigrant and underserved Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders. Recognizing that social, economic, political, and racial inequalities continue to exist in the United States, ALC is committed to the pursuit of equality and justice for all sectors of our society.

SOURCE 3 (ABC7 Bay Area) :
Judge granted request for a preliminary injunction blocking the executive order.
A federal judge in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday blocked the Trump administration's latest effort to restrict birthright citizenship for the children of international workers born in the United States, according to a newly filed ruling.
D.C. District Judge Christopher Cooper, an appointee of former President Barack Obama, granted a request for a preliminary injunction blocking President Donald Trump's executive order earlier this year that came in the wake of the Supreme Court's ruling that struck down Trump's push to formally end birthright citizenship.
Trump aimed to do away with birthright citizenship altogether in an executive order he signed on the first day of his second term last year. In August, he signed another executive order targeting birthright citizenship -- one that would outlaw what the administration has described as "birth tourism" and another that would narrow the criteria for who is eligible for birthright citizenship.
The narrower executive order directed federal agencies to not grant citizenship to children born in the U.S. to parents that lacked diplomatic immunity and who worked for foreign governments or other organizations, those born through commercial surrogacy, as well as children with a parent who is a suspected gang member or potential terrorist.
But in his ruling, Cooper said Trump "cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws" and granted the request for an injunction and class-action status from a group that filed suit who claimed their citizenship would be unlawfully denied if the order was implemented.
"The Citizenship Clause promises citizenship to practically all children born in the United States," Cooper said in the ruling. "Earlier this year, the Supreme Court kept that promise by striking down EO1. This Court does so again today by enjoining EO2’s application as to the certified class."
Trump has long called for limits to who is eligible for U.S. citizenship at birth and criticized the Supreme Court's June decision to uphold birthright citizenship. In August, he said his executive order was needed because of the high court's refusal to greenlight his earlier executive order.
"We had a very unfortunate decision in the Supreme Court concerning birthright. It was close, but a very, very unfortunate decision. So we're making adjustments because it's very unfair," Trump said at the time.
The White House denounced the ruling on Wednesday, claiming that Judge Cooper, was an "activist judge" who is "attempting to thwart President Trump’s commonsense agenda."
“This is just another ruling from an activist judge appointed by Obama attempting to thwart President Trump’s commonsense agenda. The birthright citizenship executive order is consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court," White House spokesperson said in a statement.
ABC News has reached out to the Justice Department for comment.
